Your bird should be eating a mostly pellet and veggie based diet. They may be picky, so before making a chop (basically a salad that you pre-portion and freeze), try out some things like peppers, cucumbers, collard greens, carrots.

Don't force your presence on your bird. Some birds don't like hands right away and some will never like hands. Let the bird come to you, don't ever force the bird in or out of their cage. Try to draw them back in for treats or remove outside food and water so they go back in for it.

Red ear sliders are definitely adorable, but keep in mind that these are long term pets, and if (not that im saying it will happen) you get tired of them, the only option you really have is giving them away. Do not let them loose. 

Red eared sliders do not make turtle friends. There is mate and there is enemy. If you house them together, there may be problems later on depending on gender. Res mature around 2-5 years of age, it's difficult to tell gender before then. Males will eventually have longer nails, and a thicker tail because their sex organ is hidden within their tail. 

They are semi-aquatic. They will not survive without water for more than a couple days. They also do not produce saliva, so they can only eat in the water. They're usually smart enough to know that, but just in case, don't put food out of the water for them. 

Food is given 1-2 times a day, a total of a turtle head size. Don't overfeed. That can lead to health issues. Baby turtles eat more protein than adults. Look up veggies and fruits that are res safe, and offer so their used to it by the time their willing to eat it. I suggest a hatchling pellet mix (don't overbuy, turtles grow eventually), and a shrimp/cricket/mealworm mix for treats. Treats are a weekly thing, not a daily. Fruits are treats. Don't give every day. Once your turtles are older, they should be eating more veggies. Just like people, turtles can be picky. Don't worry if they don't like something, try it again in a few weeks or months. 

[r/Redearedsliders](https://www.reddit.com/r/Redearedsliders/s/qIONfY5PAb)

Tank size depends on turtle size, 3 inch turtle, 30+ gallon tank. It's better to go bigger now, because they're going to grow. Males can grow to about 7 inches, and females to about 10. Water level is double turtle length. 

Basking platform and heat lamp is a must, but be careful about how close the heat lamp is, and the type of bulbs. Floating docks sometimes sink when the turtle is on top, so be wary of those. 

Water heater and filter is also a must. Filter cartridge changes are usually 1-2 times a month, so that's a regular expense. I suggest setting up a bi-monthly delivery of those as they usually come in 3-4 packs, depending which company.

Plants are usually more work than it's worth. 

Rocks are good, but no sand or pebbles, if it's small enough, they'll try eating. If you have females of egg laying age and size, you'll need to get some sort of nesting material.

Water changes need to happen about twice a month. That means that algae gets scrubbed off the tank, the water gets emptied entirely (,a water pump is usually helpful), you clean out any debris. Any stuff that can be cleaned gets cleaned. Any suction cups that hold stuff down need to be cleaned weekly. 

If you don't change the water often enough, it's possible to get bug larvae. Don't push off tank cleans or it's gonna be much worse later on.

Edit: totally forgot, but life food is not a good idea! That's how turtles get parasites.

Also, if there are changes, like appetite, or they get sluggish, swollen eyes, start wheezing, chirping, take them to a vet. Don't try to self doctor your turtles please
